case_name: Ahmet Özkan and Others v. Turkey
court: The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section)

facts.text: On 20 February 1993, security forces attacked the village of Ormaniçi in the Güçlükonak district of Şırnak province, resulting in the death of two children.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  The case mainly concerns events which took place in 1993 in the village of Ormaniçi in the Güçlükonak district of the Şırnak province in south-east Turkey. The applicants alleged that, on 20 February 1993, security forces had attacked Ormaniçi, as a result of which two children had died.

facts.text: On 20 February 1993, security forces set fire to houses in Ormaniçi and took most of the male villagers into detention.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants further alleged that on the same day the security forces had set fire to houses in Ormaniçi and had taken most of the male villagers into detention.

facts.text: The detained male villagers were subjected to ill-treatment in detention, resulting in serious injuries and the death of one villager.

anchor.surface_text: The applicants claimed that these men had been subjected to ill-treatment in detention, resulting in various serious injuries and the death of one villager.

facts.text: Later in 1993, security forces returned to Ormaniçi, burned houses, destroyed harvested crops, and in spring 1994 killed four villagers and forced villagers to leave.

anchor.surface_text: They further alleged that the security forces had returned to Ormaniçi later in 1993, when they had burned houses and destroyed harvested crops, and that they had returned once again in the spring of 1994 when they had killed four villagers and forced the villagers to leave Ormaniçi.

facts.text: On 20 February 1993, military forces attacked Ormaniçi early morning; soldiers wore white camouflage; there was snow and cold weather.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  In the early morning of 20 February 1993, military forces attacked the village of Ormaniçi. Many soldiers were dressed in white camouflage gear. There was snow on the ground and it was very cold.

facts.text: Military forces attacked Ormaniçi with rifles and heavy weaponry, removed families from houses to village square; many families lacked proper clothing or shoes.

anchor.surface_text: The military forces started attacking the village with rifles and heavy weaponry and later moved into the village, systematically removing each family from their house and taking them to the village square. Many families were unable to dress and were forced into the open with their children without proper clothing and/or shoes.

facts.text: Most male villagers were beaten when taken to village square, made to lie face down in mud and snow, and blindfolded; women and children assembled but not blindfolded.

anchor.surface_text: Most of the male villagers were beaten as they were taken to the village square, where they were made to lie face down in the mud and snow, and were subsequently blindfolded. The villagers arrived in the square between 10 a.m. and 12 noon and remained there until just before sunset. The women and children were also assembled near the village square but were not blindfolded.

facts.text: During the raid, soldiers conducted detailed searches and systematically set fire to homes using incendiary agents; many animals were shot or burned.

anchor.surface_text: While the villagers were being gathered in the square, a detailed search of all the properties was conducted and the soldiers began systematically setting fire to the homes, using an incendiary agent that they appeared to have brought with them specifically for this purpose. Many of the animals which were kept in stables or were wandering around the village were shot, or burned in their stables.

facts.text: A soldier threw a bomb into Mevlüde Ekin's house, injuring her six-year-old daughter Abide severely; they were evacuated to the village square.

anchor.surface_text: During the raid one soldier threw a bomb into the house of a villager called Mevlüde Ekin. The bomb exploded, causing severe intestinal injuries to her six-year-old-daughter Abide. Ms Ekin and her other children, together with Abide, were then evacuated to the village square.

facts.text: The village muhtar Mehmet Aslan was taken to Mevlüde Ekin's house to accompany soldiers in a search; a soldier inside was shot and killed; army commander instructed Mehmet Aslan to claim he was shot by terrorists.

anchor.surface_text: The village muhtar, Mehmet Aslan, was taken to the house of Mevlüde Ekin to accompany the soldiers in a search. It was claimed that somebody had been shooting from her house at the soldiers when the bomb was thrown. During this search a soldier inside the house was shot and killed instantaneously. The army commander instructed Mehmet Aslan to indicate that he had been shot by terrorists, whereas he had in fact been shot by another soldier.

facts.text: About twelve blindfolded people, including Halime Ekin, were taken by helicopter from Ormaniçi to Şırnak and placed in custody.

anchor.surface_text: Just before sunset about twelve people who had been blindfolded, including Mevlüde Ekin's daughter Halime Ekin, were taken from Ormaniçi to Şırnak by helicopter. They were placed in custody in Şırnak.

facts.text: Remaining men were roped together, forced to walk blindfolded and inadequately clothed for 7 km in snow to Güçlükonak, taking 2.5 hours.

anchor.surface_text: The remainder of the men were roped together and forced to walk blindfolded and, in many cases, without adequate clothing or footwear, from Ormaniçi to Güçlükonak. They had to walk some 7 kilometres in the snow, which took 2½ hours.

facts.text: In Güçlükonak, men were detained in a partly constructed military building with wet floors, no heating or furniture, many unfed for days, and subjected to systematic torture including electric shocks, beatings, and anal rape.

anchor.surface_text: When the men arrived in Güçlükonak, they were put into a partly constructed military building. The floors were wet and constantly under water to a depth of about 10 cm. There was no heating or furniture. Many of the men were not fed for several days. They were systematically tortured and forced, whilst blindfolded, to fingerprint statements which had been prepared for them. They suffered various forms of torture including electric shock treatment, burning with hot metal bars, beatings, and anal rape with a truncheon and with bottles.

facts.text: Many men suffered severe foot injuries from the walk and detention conditions, some requiring amputation; men were moved to Şırnak by helicopter around 5 March 1993.

anchor.surface_text: As a result of the walk to Güçlükonak and the conditions of detention there, many of the men suffered severe injuries to their feet, some of which required subsequent amputation of toes or feet. The men at Güçlükonak were moved to Şırnak by helicopter on or about 5 March 1993.

facts.text: Detained persons taken directly to Şırnak were also tortured and forced to sign statements; one man, İbrahim Ekinci, died of pneumonia in hospital on 16 March 1993 after torture.

anchor.surface_text: The persons who had been taken directly to Şırnak were also tortured and forced to sign statements. Allegations were put to them that they were members or supporters of the PKK. One man, İbrahim Ekinci, having been tortured, fell ill and was removed to hospital, where he died of pneumonia on 16 March 1993.

facts.text: On 21 February 1993, military forces returned to Ormaniçi to burn more houses and kill more animals; villagers sheltered in mosque, caves, and unburned buildings.

anchor.surface_text: On 21 February 1993, military forces returned to Ormaniçi to burn more houses and kill more animals. The women of the village, together with the children, slept in the mosque, in caves, and in some unburned outbuildings.

facts.text: Abide Ekin died in the mosque without medical attention; another child, Ali Yıldırım, was killed by explosion of mortar bomb or grenade left by military forces.

anchor.surface_text: Abide Ekin died in the mosque, without having received medical attention for her injuries. A few days later, another child, Ali Yıldırım, was killed as a result of the explosion of a mortar bomb or grenade that had been left in the village by the military forces after the attack on 20 February 1993.

facts.text: Most detained villagers were released on 9 or 16 March 1993; many complained of torture to public prosecutors; some remained in custody until June 1993.

anchor.surface_text: Most of the detained villagers were released either on 9 or 16 March 1993. They appeared before public prosecutors at Eruh (Siirt district) and many complained of the torture that they had suffered. The villagers remained in custody until approximately June 1993.

facts.text: Two villagers, Mehmet Nuri Özkan and Ali Erbek, were still in custody at the time of the oral hearing in October 1998; Mehmet Nuri Özkan has since been released; Ali Erbek remains in custody.

anchor.surface_text: Two villagers, Mehmet Nuri Özkan and Ali Erbek, were still in custody at the time of the oral hearing held in October 1998. Mehmet Nuri Özkan has been released since, but Ali Erbek is currently still in custody.

facts.text: Some detained men were taken to Mardin and Diyarbakır State Hospitals for medical treatment, including amputations; Fahrettin Özkan, aged 13 at the time, was among them.

anchor.surface_text: Both before and at the time of the transfer of the men from Şırnak to Eruh a number were taken to the Mardin and Diyarbakır State Hospitals, where they were placed in the prison wing. After medical treatment, some had parts of their feet amputated. This was the case of Fahrettin Özkan, who was only 13 years old at the material time.

facts.text: At release in March 1993, most detained men were taken by bus to Siirt and then to a nearby village; many returned to Ormaniçi by mule due to inability to walk.

anchor.surface_text: At the time of their release on 9 and 13 March 1993 respectively, the majority of the detained men were taken by bus to Siirt and subsequently to a nearby village. For the most part they returned to Ormaniçi by mule since they were unable to walk.

facts.text: Between March and late 1993, many men attempted to rebuild burnt houses as they recovered from injuries.

anchor.surface_text: During the period between 9 March 1993 and the summer/autumn of 1993, as they gradually recovered from their injuries, many of the men attempted to rebuild the burnt houses.

facts.text: In late summer or autumn 1993, security forces returned to Ormaniçi, assembled villagers near the school, tortured two women, removed and destroyed harvested crops, burnt more buildings, and caused animal deaths.

anchor.surface_text: In the late summer or autumn of 1993 there was a further incident in Ormaniçi. On this occasion all the villagers were assembled near the school. Two women were taken into the school and tortured and the soldiers went to a number of houses and removed all of the harvested crops and destroyed them. Some more buildings were also burnt, and further animals died after eating contaminated food.

facts.text: Many villagers had left Ormaniçi to live in nearby caves but continued to cultivate their land.

anchor.surface_text: Many of the villagers had left the village to live in caves nearby but had continued to cultivate their land.

facts.text: In spring 1994, soldiers returned to Ormaniçi, killed four villagers and three alleged PKK members, and forced villagers to leave within three days.

anchor.surface_text: In or about May 1994 the soldiers came to the village once more and gunfire was heard in the orchards and fields nearby. After that the soldiers arrived in the village indicating that they had killed seven terrorists. In fact four villagers had been killed as well as three alleged members of the PKK. After this incident the villagers were given three days to leave the village, otherwise they would be killed.

facts.text: Villagers left Ormaniçi after the 1994 incident, moving to towns in south-east Turkey and Istanbul; they have been unable to return since.

anchor.surface_text: They all left and moved to various towns in south-east Turkey, including Güçlükonak, Tarsus and Siirt. A number also moved to İstanbul. They have been unable to return to the village since that date.

facts.text: In August 1994, the Government investigated the February 1993 events in Ormaniçi but did not investigate detention conditions or injuries; no compensation was offered to applicants.

anchor.surface_text: In August 1994 the Government carried out an investigation in Ormaniçi into the events which had taken place there in February 1993. No investigation was carried out into the detention of the villagers in Güçlükonak or Şırnak, notwithstanding the injuries they had suffered whilst in custody. None of the applicants has been offered any compensation for their losses.
Relying on Articles 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 of the Convention, the applicants complained of a military raid conducted on 20 February 1993 on the village of Ormaniçi and related events

The applicants further alleged a violation of former Article 25 (now Article 34) and former Article 28 of the Convention (now 38).

The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 16 January 1996 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999 in accordance with Article 5 § 3, second sentence, of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention, the Commission not having completed its examination of the case by that date.
Since approximately 1985 serious disturbances have raged in the south-east of Turkey between the security forces and the members of the PKK (Workers' Party of Kurdistan).

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court assessed the evidence beyond reasonable doubt, found the applicants' version credible, and concluded that the State failed to protect the right to life during the military raid.

Turkey, judgment of 16 September 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-IV, p. 1199, § 15, Menteş and Others v. Turkey, judgment of 28 November 1997, Reports 1997-VIII, p. 2696, § 13, Ertak v. Turkey, no. 20764/92, § 131, ECHR 2000-V, and Taş v. Turkey, no. 24396/94, § 11, ECHR 2000-XI).

outcome.relief_summary: The Court found violations of Articles 2 (procedural), 3 (substantive and procedural), 5 (multiple aspects), and 8, granting pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages to the applicants. Some aspects of Articles 2 and 3 were found not violated. The Court awarded just satisfaction under Article 41.
directions: The Court directed the respondent State to conduct effective investigations into the violations found, particularly regarding the deaths and ill-treatment.
The State was to pay just satisfaction to the applicants as awarded by the Court.
The Court emphasized the need for the State to ensure compliance with Convention rights in similar circumstances in the future.
